investigacion.base:
Based on current information, the most likely count is about **6–8 launches** (center around 7). The resolution window is October 16–31, 2026 UTC, and no launches have happened in it yet.

**What the resolution source says**
- The Wikipedia list says that as of October 2, 2026, rockets from the Falcon 9 family have been launched 706 times, with 703 full mission successes, two mission failures during launch, one mission failure before launch, and one partial failure. I couldn't see the 2026 table row by row. The Edit warring, Consensus and Metaculus FAQ pages are standard policy pages and have no bearing on the count.

**Recent launches**
- Oct 1: Crew-13 lifted off from Cape pad 40, and Transporter-18, carrying 130 payloads, flew from Vandenberg pad 4E at 1832 UTC.
- Oct 2: Falcon Heavy launched NROL-97 from Kennedy Space Center (success).
- Oct 5: the SDA Tranche 1 Transport Layer A launch aborted in the countdown's final minute, for reasons that the company has not disclosed. It flew on Oct 10 at 0739 GMT.
- Space.com calls SLC-4E currently SpaceX's only launch facility on the West Coast. SpaceX also launched the first Starlink V3 satellites on Starship in late September, which may take some Starlink work away from Falcon.

**2026 pace (base rate)**
- The Falcon family's 100th launch of 2026 flew from Cape Canaveral on August 21, putting the company on pace for roughly 160 launches this year. That's about 0.43 launches a day, or roughly **6.9 per 16 days**.
- Gwynne Shotwell said the company expects approximately 140 to 145 Falcon 9 launches in 2026. That works out to about 6.1–6.4 per 16 days.
- One source says pad capacity limits the theoretical 2026 annual maximum to roughly 155 to 165 total launches. If that's right, 9 or more launches in 16 days would be unusual.
- Last year's pace was higher: in late 2025, SpaceX often flew 7–10 Falcon launches in a 16-day stretch.

**Scheduled launches in the window**
- USSF-481 on Falcon 9 from Vandenberg was listed for Oct 19 (per NextSpaceflight, 10 days ago).
- Bandwagon-5 from the Cape is listed as "no earlier than" October.
- The rest are likely to be regular Starlink launches, which are usually announced only a few days ahead.

**Risks that would lower the count:** an anomaly that grounds Falcon 9, weather or Atlantic/Pacific recovery conditions, and the undisclosed cause of the Oct 5 abort.

**Prediction markets:** I didn't find any market on this specific window. A Polymarket-style market seen in about April 2026 priced 140–159 total 2026 launches at about 35%, with about $246K traded. It's old and only loosely relevant.

**Sources:**

- [6](https://keeptrack.space/x-report/spacex-brief-2026-08-22)
- [7](https://newspaceeconomy.ca/2026/04/05/maximum-theoretical-falcon-9-launch-rate-for-spacex-in-2026/)

criterios: This question resolves as the number of launches of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launch vehicles occurring between October 16, 2026 and October 31, 2026 (inclusive of both dates and in UTC), according to Wikipedia's [List of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy launches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Falcon_9_and_Falcon_Heavy_launches#2026).

(a) **Time remaining:** The October 16–31 UTC counting window begins in four days. The outcome will be known after October 31, about 20 days from today.

(b) **Status quo:** No launches have occurred in the window yet. If SpaceX maintains its recent cadence, roughly six or seven launches is the central expectation.

(c) **Base rates:** A pace of 140–160 Falcon-family launches per year implies about six to seven launches in 16 days. That puts five or six and seven or more ahead of the lower-count options, though short windows can vary considerably.

(d) **Unexpected outcome:** A launch anomaly that temporarily grounds Falcon 9, or several weather-related delays, could bring the count down to four or fewer.

Option_A: 4%
Option_B: 18%
Option_C: 35%
Option_D: 43%

(a) **Time until resolution.** The window runs October 16–31, 2026 UTC. It opens in about 4 days and closes in about 19 days. Wikipedia normally updates within hours of each launch.

(b) **Status quo.** At the recent cadence, SpaceX flies roughly 6–7 Falcon launches per 16 days.
- The 100 launches by August 21 imply about 0.43 per day, or about 6.9 per 16 days.
- The Wikipedia total of 706 as of October 2 hints at a slowdown since August, to perhaps 0.35–0.4 per day.
- Shotwell's guidance of 140–145 launches for the year implies about 6.1–6.4 per 16 days.
- Starship has begun flying Starlink V3, which may take some Starlink work off Falcon.
- USSF-481 (about October 19) and possibly Bandwagon-5 are listed in or near the window; the rest would mostly be Starlink.

So the status quo lands at the 5–6 / 7+ boundary.

(c) **Base rates.**
- In late 2025, SpaceX often flew 7–10 launches per 16 days.
- In 2026 the average is about 6–7 per 16 days, possibly drifting lower.
- Launch counts vary less than random chance would predict because SpaceX schedules steadily. Still, weather, recovery-ship conditions and pad turnarounds produce swings of about ±2.
- Groundings have been rare (2024 brought a couple of short stand-downs of about 1–2 weeks). Each one has a few-percent chance of overlapping any given 16-day window.

(d) **Unexpected scenarios.**
- A Falcon 9 anomaly, such as an upper-stage failure, grounds the fleet for 1–2 weeks. The count would then drop to 2 or fewer, or 3–4.
- Starship taking over Starlink deployment faster than expected thins the Falcon manifest to 3–4.
- Conversely, a backlog of Starlink missions flushed out after the early-October delays, flying from all three pads, could push the count to 8 or more.

Final probabilities:

Option_A: 6
Option_B: 19
Option_C: 40
Option_D: 35

**(a) Time left:** The window begins October 16 and ends October 31, UTC. The count should be known in about 19 days.

**(b) Status quo:** No launches have occurred in the window yet, so a literal halt would mean **Two or fewer**. If SpaceX continues its normal launch cadence, roughly six or seven launches is more plausible.

**(c) Base rates:** A pace of 140–160 Falcon launches per year implies about 6.1–7.0 launches per 16 days. That puts **Five or Six** and **Seven or more** ahead of the lower brackets. The scheduled missions offer some support, but most Starlink launches will not be firmly scheduled this far out.

**(d) Unexpected outcome:** A rocket anomaly or prolonged bad recovery weather could ground launches for much of the window and produce **Two or fewer**.

Option_A: 5%
Option_B: 18%
Option_C: 31%
Option_D: 46%
